title: Neutralisation: acid meets base
body: In water, an acid gives off hydrogen ions (H⁺), tiny charged particles. A base like sodium hydroxide gives off hydroxide ions (OH⁻). When they meet, they join up to make water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
Each drop of base uses up some of the acid's H⁺ ions. But the liquid stays acidic until every one has been used up. Here, 25 mL of acid needs exactly 25 mL of base of the same strength.

That exact point is called the equivalence point, and the liquid is neutral: pH 7. A few more drops leave spare OH⁻ ions. So the pH shoots up and the liquid turns basic. It's like filling a glass to the brim: one more drop and it spills over.
equation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O (acid + base → salt + water)
realWorld: Farmers spread lime, a base, on soil that has become too acidic. Antacid tablets cancel out extra stomach acid. In both cases the amount matters, because too much base overshoots and makes things basic.
